You build an argument: you introduce points, concede, object and draw conclusions (certes… mais, en revanche, pourtant, c’est pourquoi).
Admittedly, the hall was expensive, but it will serve for fifty years.
On the one hand it’s useful; on the other hand it isn’t expensive.
Although I agree, I have a question.
On the other hand, the roads are in poor condition.
That’s why I’m voting for this project.
To introduce and order arguments: d’abord, ensuite, d’une part… d’autre part, de plus.
To concede a point to your opponent: certes… mais, il est vrai que… mais, bien que + subjunctive.
To express opposition: en revanche, pourtant, néanmoins, au contraire.
To draw a conclusion: donc, c’est pourquoi, par conséquent, en somme.
To take part in a polite debate: Permettez-moi de…, Je ne suis pas d’accord avec vous sur ce point.

Wednesday, 18 September 2029, two days before the inauguration. The station “Radio Lyon” holds a debate: should public money fund music for children? Face to face: Claire Vasseur, director of the Conservatoire, and Bernard Delorme, an opposition city councillor and Marc Delorme’s uncle.
Good evening. Tonight, a simple question: should public money fund music for children? Mr Delorme, you voted against the project. Why?
First, I want to say that I love music. But on the one hand, the city is in debt. On the other hand, there are priorities: roads, schools, safety. That’s why I voted against.
Admittedly, the city is in debt. But the hall wasn’t paid for with the taxes of Lyon’s residents: sixty per cent was funded by the region and twenty per cent by private donations.
The region is taxpayers’ money too, madam. There’s no magic money.

You’re right on that point. Nevertheless, I’d like to give you a figure. Since the start of the project, absenteeism at the La Duchère school has fallen by fifteen per cent. The children come to school because they have rehearsal afterwards.
That’s a good figure, I admit. Yet a sports school might have given the same result, for less money.
Perhaps. But it isn’t one or the other. On the contrary: half of our children also play football. Although music costs more at the start, a violin lasts fifty years.
Mr Delorme, a delicate question. Your nephew, Marc Delorme, allegedly wrote the false article about the hall. Did you know?
(silence) No. And I deeply regret it. Let me be clear: you can disagree with a project, but you have no right to lie. I apologise to the project team.
Thank you, Mr Delorme. I greatly respect what you have just said. And I invite you on Friday. Come and listen to the children, and then criticise us if you like.
I accept. But I warn you: I won’t change my mind easily.
In short, you disagree on the budget, but you agree on the truth. That’s already a lot. Thank you both.
(“il n’y a pas” = there is no)
(“au contraire” = on the contrary; “au départ” = at the start)
(“être au courant” = to know, to be aware)
come (“venir de” = to have just done)
A convincing speech is ORDERED. Connectors help the listener follow the ideas:
D’abord, la ville a des dettes.
De plus, il y a des priorités.
D’une part, c’est utile ; d’autre part, ce n’est pas cher.
“En outre” (furthermore) is formal and written. In speech, “de plus” or “en plus” sound more natural.
2. Concession: you grant a point, then contradict it
The strongest weapon in a debate: you agree with your opponent on ONE point, the better to contradict them:
Admittedly, the city is in debt. But the hall wasn’t paid for with taxes.
It’s true that it’s expensive, but it’s useful.
You’re right on that point. Nevertheless…
Although music costs more, a violin lasts fifty years.
“Bien que” requires the SUBJUNCTIVE: “bien que je SOIS d’accord”, “bien qu’il AIT raison”, “bien que ça COÛTE cher”. The typical mistake: “bien que je suis” ✗.
Il a raison. Pourtant, je ne suis pas convaincu.
C’est un bon chiffre. Néanmoins, c’est cher.
Les écoles vont bien. En revanche, les routes…
Ce n’est pas l’un ou l’autre. Au contraire !
Il veut des routes, alors qu’elle veut des violons.
“En revanche” compares two DIFFERENT things (schools vs roads). “Pourtant” shows an unexpected contradiction within the SAME thing.
Il ment, donc je ne le crois pas.
Par conséquent, le projet est utile.
En somme, vous êtes d’accord sur la vérité.
“Bref” is very common in speech, at the end of a long explanation: “Bref, c’était une catastrophe.”
Je ne suis pas d’accord avec vous sur ce point.
I don’t agree with you on that point.
Vous avez raison sur ce point, mais…
You’re right on that point, but…
The French love debating and interrupt each other often. “Laissez-moi finir” is a phrase you will hear on any political programme.

He’s right. Yet I’m not convinced.

On Friday 20 September, Ioana woke up before the alarm. It was half past five. Outside it was still dark, but the sky was clear, without a single cloud. She lay still for a while, listening to Julien’s breathing and, in the next room, the little sounds of Rose-Hélène talking in her sleep.

She was thinking of Hélène. Of course, Hélène wouldn’t be there. Yet Ioana felt that, in a way, the whole day belonged to her. It was Hélène who had wanted music to reach the neighbourhoods. It was her money that paid for the scholarship. And it was her waltz the children were going to play.

At nine, Odile left for Part-Dieu station, in her Sunday coat, to meet Isabelle. She refused to let Julien go with her. “I’m fetching my daughter on my own,” she said. “I’m only seventy-nine.” Julien didn’t argue. You didn’t argue with Odile, any more than with Lucien Roux.

Isabelle got off the train with a small suitcase and a large parcel wrapped in brown paper. Her hair was grey now, cut very short, and she had her father’s eyes, according to Odile. The two women hugged for a long time on the platform, without saying anything, while travellers walked around them.

“What’s that parcel?” Odile asked in the taxi. “You’ll see,” Isabelle replied. “It’s for the hall. Although it’s a bit late, I think Dad would have agreed.” Odile tried to touch the parcel, but Isabelle put it on the other side, like when she was little and used to hide the Christmas presents.

At La Duchère, since the morning, the whole neighbourhood had been outside. The mothers had made cakes, oriental pastries, tarts. Mr Mansouri had set up a big table under the lime tree and put three teapots on it. Mrs Mansouri was handing out glasses of mint tea to everyone who passed, invited or not.

Mihaela had come from Fourvière with her țambal, carried by two people from the care home, Mr Petit, ninety-four, and a young nurse. Mr Petit had insisted on carrying his side of the instrument. “I carried mail bags for forty years,” he said. “A Romanian piano isn’t going to scare me.”

Around four, the official guests started to arrive. The mayor, Claire Vasseur, regional councillors, Pierre Duval with his notebook. And, a little apart, a man in a grey suit who hesitated to come in: Bernard Delorme. He had come, as he had promised on the radio. Nobody really knew what to say to him.

An old lady solved the problem. She got up from the front row, took him by the arm and sat him down next to her. “I’m Jeanne,” she said. “I’m the one who wrote to you in the paper. I promised you a seat. My grandson plays the violin. The third one, on the left. You’ll tell me what you think.”

At five o’clock sharp, the mayor took the floor. He spoke about the city, the region, the neighbourhoods, the budget. He thanked everyone, twice. The children were starting to fidget on their chairs. Yanis was counting the panes of the ceiling window. Inès was checking the reed of her clarinet for the tenth time.

Then it was Radu’s turn. He had prepared a three-page speech. He took it out of his pocket, looked at it, and put it back in his pocket. “First,” he said, “I’d like to say that I’m not a great speaker. Next, you’re hungry, and the cakes are outside. Finally, the children have better things to say than I do. So I’ll be brief.”

The hall laughed. “A year ago,” Radu went on, “a ten-year-old boy drew me a window in the roof, because he wanted to see the sky while he played. I was told it was too expensive, too complicated, too dangerous. It’s true that it was expensive. It’s true that it was complicated. Nevertheless, look up.”

Three hundred people looked up at the same time. The late-afternoon sun came through the big pane and drew a golden rectangle on the parquet, right where the orchestra was sitting. Someone clapped, then everyone. Radu went back to his seat, red to the ears. He had spoken for a minute and a half.

Julien stood up. He had no baton; he had never needed one with the children. He simply looked at each musician, one by one, and smiled. Then he gave Inès a small nod. The clarinet began alone, very softly, the first notes of Henri’s waltz.

At the second verse the violins came in, then Yanis’s red cello, then Mihaela’s țambal, which gave the waltz the flavour of a village feast. And at the third verse, as planned, Odile stood up in the front row and whistled the melody, with the children, louder than the violins, exactly as she had promised Radu.

Isabelle was crying. Mrs Roux was crying. Mr Petit pretended he had a speck of dust in his eye. And Bernard Delorme, sitting next to Jeanne, was watching the third violin on the left without moving, his hands clenched on his knees. At the end, Jeanne leaned towards him. “Well?” He took a long time to answer. “He plays out of tune,” he said at last. “But he plays with his heart.”

After the concert, everyone went outside in front of the hall, under the lime tree. On the façade, the plaque was still hidden under its white sheet. The mayor coughed, asked for silence, and beckoned to Rose-Hélène. Julien carried her to the wall. She took the corner of the sheet in her little hand and pulled with all her strength.

The sheet fell. On the pale stone plaque one could read: “Hélène Morel Hall (1942-2029). She waited all her life. Thanks to her, children will wait no more.” Below, engraved small, were a few musical notes: the first four bars of the waltz.

There was a great silence. Then the children cheered, all together, as if for a goal at football. So the rumour was true. Mrs Roux told everyone she had always known. Julien confessed that he was the one who had proposed the sentence. The mayor, for his part, confessed he had found it very hard to keep the secret.

It was at that moment that Isabelle undid the brown paper of her parcel. Inside was a frame, and in the frame, an old black-and-white photo: a young sailor, in uniform, laughing on the deck of a ship. He was holding a harmonica in his right hand. His left hand, injured, was hidden in his pocket.

“That’s my father,” Isabelle said. “In 1971, the year he met my mother. He used to say the harmonica was the only instrument you can play with one hand. For years I thought he didn’t like music. In reality, he loved it too much. I’d like this photo to hang in the hall, next to Hélène’s. Although they never saw each other again, I think they should be together here.”

Odile took the frame from her daughter’s hands and looked at it for a long time. Then she said, in a voice nobody had heard from her before: “He only laughed like that when he was on the water. Or when he whistled the waltz.” She gave the frame back to Julien, and went to sit under the lime tree, alone, for a long while.

Meanwhile, Bernard Delorme had come up to Radu. He looked embarrassed, like a pupil sent to the headmaster. “Mr Popescu,” he said, “I want to be honest with you. Admittedly, I haven’t changed my mind about the budget. I still think the city has other priorities.”

“On the other hand,” he went on, “I have changed my mind about something else. I thought these children needed jobs, not violins. I was wrong. On the one hand, they work harder than I do. On the other hand, the violin is work.” He took an envelope out of his jacket. “It’s personal. Not the town hall, not my party. For the orchestra’s coach trips.”

Radu took the envelope without knowing what to say. Delorme hesitated, then added, more quietly: “My nephew is outside. He didn’t dare come in. He would like to speak to you, if you’ll allow it. I’m not asking you to forgive him. I’m only asking you to listen to him for five minutes.”

Marc Delorme was waiting by the bins, at the corner of the street, hands in his pockets. He was younger than Radu had imagined, twenty-five perhaps, with a badly shaved beard and tired eyes. When he saw Radu coming, he stepped back, as if he expected to be hit.

“I’m not going to hit you,” Radu said. “I’m an architect, not a boxer.” Marc almost smiled. Then he told him everything, very fast, without looking at Radu. His father’s company had lost the tender. His father had had to lay off six people. He was angry, he was looking for someone to blame. A worker had told him about the roof problem, and he had written the article in one night.

“I made up the rest,” he admitted. “The budget, the intern, everything. I thought nobody would read it. And then I saw the video, with the little girl and the clarinet. I watched it twenty times. I haven’t slept since.” He looked up for the first time. “I’m sorry. Truly.”

Radu looked at him for a long time. He thought of Inès, of the fear in her eyes, of the terrible comments. He could have been angry. He would have been right to be angry. Yet all he felt was tiredness, and something that looked a little like pity. He knew the fear of losing a project only too well.

“You can write,” Radu said at last. “That’s something. So write. But write the truth. The orchestra needs someone to tell its year in the neighbourhood paper. There’s no money, it’s volunteer work. Rehearsals are on Wednesdays.” Marc looked at him without understanding. “Are you serious?” “I’m Romanian,” Radu replied. “Where I come from, we always give a second chance. Not a third.”

When Radu came back under the lime tree, the party had started. Mr Mansouri was playing the oud, Mihaela accompanied him on the țambal, and a boy was trying to keep up on the drum. It sounded like nothing anyone knew, neither Arab music, nor Romanian music, nor French music. It was, in short, the music of La Duchère.

Rose-Hélène was dancing among the children, spinning around until she fell, then getting up and starting again, laughing. Ioana watched her, sitting on the bench next to Odile. “Do you know what Hélène told me, the last time?” Odile whispered. “She told me: I want to see Rose-Hélène walk. She saw her walk. Today she sees her dance.”

A little further away, Bernard Delorme was sitting on a plastic chair, a glass of tea in his hand, next to Jeanne’s grandson. The boy was showing him how to hold a bow. The councillor was trying, without success, to the children’s laughter. “You see?” Jeanne said as she passed. “It isn’t so easy. Consequently, it’s real work.” Delorme raised his hands, as if to say he surrendered.

Late that evening, when the last guests had left, Pierre Duval still had his notebook open. He came to see Radu one last time. “I’ve got my headline for tomorrow,” he said. “Do you want to hear it?” Radu nodded. The journalist read aloud: “La Duchère: the hall that only lets the light through.”

Radu smiled. Then he closed the door of the hall, switched off the light, and stayed a while in the dark. Through the big ceiling window you could see the stars. He thought of Lucia, of May, of the wedding, of don Manuel and doña Carmen, who were going to fly for the first time. He thought that the waltz, after all, wasn’t over. It was only just beginning.

After the debate, “Lyon Matin” publishes listeners’ letters. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.
Courrier des lecteurs : la musique, un luxe ?
I listened carefully to Wednesday evening’s debate on Radio Lyon. I would like to respond, because I am at once a taxpayer, a grandmother and a former primary-school teacher in La Duchère.
First, I understand Mr Delorme. It is true that the city is in debt, and it is normal for an elected official to ask about the cost. I pay my taxes too, and I don’t like my money being wasted.

Yet for thirty years I saw children leave school without knowing what they loved. Some had never succeeded at anything, and nobody had ever applauded them. On the other hand, last year I saw my grandson play the violin in front of three hundred people.

Although I am not an economist, I can count. A child who loves school costs society less than a child who drops out. On the one hand, they find work more easily; on the other hand, they are less likely to go off the rails.

Finally, I would like to thank Mr Delorme for his apology. It is rare for a politician to admit a mistake on the radio. That is why I hope he will come on Friday. He will sit next to me, if he wishes.

In short, music is not a luxury. It is a bridge between children and school, between neighbourhoods and the city, between generations. And bridges, in Lyon, we know what they are worth. — Jeanne R., La Duchère

(“mal tourner” = to go off the rails)

Dear Sir or Madam, I would like to respond to your article about the closure of the theatre in my neighbourhood.
Admittedly, the theatre costs the city a lot, and it is true that the hall is often half empty.
Yet it is the only cultural venue in the neighbourhood. On the one hand, schools hold their shows there; on the other hand, elderly people come there on Sundays.
Although I understand the budget problems, I think other solutions must be sought.
That is why I propose a volunteer association. In short, closing the theatre would cost more than keeping it.
